Court
KōRT
n. (rendering Hebrew chātsēr and Greek aulē)
From Old French cort, from Latin cohors, an enclosure or yard and thence the company of people gathered in it — the same root that gives cohort. Both senses ride in the English word: a court is a walled open space, and a court is the retinue of a king. Hebrew chātsēr is the enclosed yard of the tabernacle and temple, and the word carries the plain sense of an enclosure with hangings around it.

Biblical Definition

The courts are the outer enclosure of God's house, and their whole doctrinal significance lies in their being outer. The tabernacle's court was a hundred cubits of fine twined linen hung on pillars (Exo 27:9), containing the brasen altar and the laver, and it was as far as the ordinary Israelite could come. Beyond it lay the holy place, where only priests entered, and the holiest of all, entered once a year by one man with blood. The court therefore taught access and its limits in the plainest possible architecture: you may come, and you may come this far, and there is a sacrifice standing between you and any nearer approach. Given that, the psalmists' language about the courts is astonishing in its warmth. “My soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the LORD” (Psa 84:2); a day in thy courts is better than a thousand; “Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise” (Psa 100:4). The blessedness of Psa 65:4 is expressly a chosen and caused approach — blessed is the man whom thou choosest, and causest to approach unto thee, that he may dwell in thy courts — which is election and effectual calling stated in the language of temple architecture. The New Testament completes it: the veil is rent, the way into the holiest is made manifest, and believers now have boldness to enter by the blood of Jesus. The longing of the psalmist for the court is answered by an access he did not have.

Webster 1828 Definition

The walled outer enclosure of the tabernacle and temple, containing the altar and laver and marking the limit of the ordinary worshipper's approach; in the psalms the object of longing and thanksgiving, and the architectural picture of an access that Christ has since opened to the holiest itself.

expand to see more

COURT, n. 1. A space inclosed by walls and open above, as before a house, or in the middle of a building.

2. In Scripture, the inclosed area of the tabernacle and of the temple. Thou shalt make the court of the tabernacle. Exod. 27.

3. The persons who compose the retinue of a prince or sovereign; whence the word is used both of the place and of the company assembled in it.

4. A place where justice is administered; the hall or chamber in which judges sit; and the judges themselves in session.

5. In the temple of Herod there were several courts; that of the Gentiles, that of the women, that of Israel, and that of the priests, each nearer than the last to the holy place.

Key Scripture

Psalm 84:2 — "My soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the LORD: my heart and my flesh crieth out for the living God."

Psalm 100:4 — "Enter into his gates with thanksgiving, and into his courts with praise: be thankful unto him, and bless his name."

Exodus 27:9 — "And thou shalt make the court of the tabernacle: for the south side southward there shall be hangings for the court of fine twined linen of an hundred cubits long for one side:"

Psalm 65:4 — "Blessed is the man whom thou choosest, and causest to approach unto thee, that he may dwell in thy courts: we shall be satisfied with the goodness of thy house, even of thy holy temple."

Modern Corruption

The graded courts are treated as a relic of primitive religion that the gospel simply abolished, so that the modern worshipper loses both the seriousness of approach and any sense that access to God cost anything.

expand to see more

The tabernacle's architecture was a sermon on the holiness of God, and where it is dismissed as mere ancient ritual the sermon is unpreached. The rending of the veil did not teach that the graded approach had always been an unnecessary severity; it taught that the barrier was real and that Christ had removed it at the cost of His flesh. Hebrews reasons precisely this way — the way into the holiest was not yet made manifest while the first tabernacle was standing — so the old arrangement is treated as a true statement of the problem, and the new as the true solution. A worship that has lost the courts tends to lose reverence first and then to lose the cross, since a God who was never inaccessible needed no one to open the way.

There is a corresponding error in the other direction, and it recurs whenever churches reintroduce graded holy space — a sanctuary the people may not enter, a table only clergy may approach, an altar rail treated as the boundary of the holy. The New Testament makes the whole congregation a holy priesthood with boldness to enter. To rebuild the partition in stone or in practice is to build again the thing Christ destroyed. The right recovery is neither the abolition of reverence nor the restoration of the veil, but the astonishment Hebrews expects: having therefore boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus…let us draw near.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chātsēr is the enclosed yard of the sanctuary and also, in another sense, a settled village. Greek aulē covers the courtyard of a house or palace, the temple court, and the sheepfold.

expand to see more

Hebrew chātsēr (H2691) — a court, an enclosure; the court of the tabernacle and the courts of the LORD's house; the same form also denotes an unwalled village.

Hebrew 'āzārâh (H5835) — an enclosed space, a ledge or court; used of the courts of Ezekiel's temple and of the great court of 2Ch 4:9.

Greek aulē (G833) — a courtyard, palace court, fold; the high priest's palace where Peter denied the Lord (Mat 26:69), and the sheepfold of Joh 10:1.

Greek hieron (G2411) — the temple with its whole precinct and courts, as distinguished from naos, the sanctuary proper — a distinction the Authorized Version does not mark in English.

Greek parrhēsia (G3954) — boldness, freedom of speech and access; the word of Heb 10:19, the new standing that the old courts anticipated and could not give.

Usage

"Of the tabernacle and temple structure: the court of the tabernacle with its hangings of fine twined linen (Exo 27:9); the inner court and the great court (1Ki 6:36; 7:12)."

"Of the worshipper's longing and thanksgiving: my soul fainteth for the courts of the LORD (Psa 84:2); enter into his courts with praise (Psa 100:4)."

"Of a chosen and caused approach: blessed is the man whom thou choosest, and causest to approach unto thee (Psa 65:4)."
